case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court may certify a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class that includes class members who suffered no Article III injury (i.e., are “uninjured” and thus lack standing).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (standing/injury-in-fact requirement) as applied through Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3) class-certification requirements (predominance/superiority).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Labcorp argues that Article III limits federal judicial power to resolving claims of parties who have suffered a concrete injury, so a damages class that affirmatively includes uninjured members is improper because it (1) exceeds the court’s jurisdiction by purporting to adjudicate claims for persons without standing, and (2) undermines Rule 23(b)(3) predominance/superiority by necessitating individualized injury inquiries and creating overbroad, settlement-coercive aggregate liability. Labcorp also emphasizes that the Supreme Court reviews the judgment, not lower-court reasoning or particular class-definition phrasing, and thus can reverse the Ninth Circuit’s affirmance of certification even if the class definition evolved below.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend the certified classes were comprised of people injured by disability discrimination and that the Ninth Circuit correctly affirmed certification; to the extent any class members might ultimately fail to prove injury, that is a merits/claims-administration issue handled at later stages (e.g., through individualized proof, claims processes, or excluding non-qualifying members), not a categorical Article III bar to class certification. They frame the case as about remedying discrimination against individuals with disabilities rather than authorizing recovery by truly uninjured persons.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that TransUnion expressly reserved the timing question and that a feasible, court-supervised winnowing process can sometimes ensure no uninjured person recovers. But where, as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett emphasize, the class as certified and the plaintiffs’ proof model affirmatively sweep in substantial numbers of uninjured members without a workable classwide method to identify injury, individualized standing becomes central and predominance/superiority fail—this is not something that can be cured by post-certification “claims administration” without recreating mini-trials. Justice Sotomayor is right to worry about foreclosing small-claim aggregation, yet our narrow course is to vacate and remand for a rigorous Rule 23(b)(3) and Article III analysis consistent with TransUnion, without announcing a categorical, across-the-board timing rule. That approach respects TransUnion’s reservation while preventing Rule 23 from being used, in practical effect, to generate settlement pressure untethered to the court’s power to award damages.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s reliance on TransUnion’s reservation about timing does not answer the antecedent constitutional problem: a federal court may exercise judicial power only in a concrete “Case,” and certification is the court’s authorization to litigate and exert settlement leverage on behalf of absent persons. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, when the class as defined and supported at certification affirmatively includes substantial numbers of uninjured members without a workable, classwide method to identify injury, individualized standing inquiries become central—undermining Rule 23(b)(3) predominance and implicating the Rules Enabling Act’s bar on using procedure to enlarge substantive limits. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s proposal to “screen later” is inadequate where the standing defect is baked into the class theory itself; TransUnion’s reservation leaves room only for administrable mechanisms that do not require merits-like, individualized injury mini-trials to determine who may recover. A narrow vacate-and-remand, grounded in these Article III and Rule 23 constraints rather than a categorical timing rule, remains the sound institutional disposition.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that TransUnion reserved the timing question and that claims administration can later screen out uninjured members—does not justify certifying a (b)(3) damages class whose definition affirmatively sweeps in substantial numbers of persons who could not sue for damages in federal court. As the Chief Justice notes, that is not a mere downstream distribution issue; it goes to Rule 23(b)(3) predominance and superiority because individualized injury-in-fact inquiries become central if injury cannot be established with common proof or an administrable, ex ante method. Allowing certification first and sorting standing later would use Rule 23 to generate settlement pressure and effectively adjudicate claims beyond Article III limits, contrary to the Rules Enabling Act’s command that the Rules cannot enlarge substantive (including jurisdictional) constraints. I agree with Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett that a narrow vacatur and remand—requiring rigorous predominance/administrability analysis consistent with TransUnion—respects TransUnion’s reservation without permitting overinclusive damages classes to proceed on the hope that jurisdictional defects can be cured at the back end.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh raise the most serious point: an overinclusive (b)(3) damages class can create settlement pressure and signal that individualized injury issues defeat predominance. But that concern is properly handled through rigorous Rule 23(b)(3) predominance/superiority/manageability—requiring, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, a concrete, court-supervised plan to winnow out uninjured members before any damages award—rather than converting TransUnion’s “standing to recover” into a categorical certification-stage constitutional bar that TransUnion expressly reserved. Justice Thomas’s premise that certification itself exceeds Article III overstates what certification does and would, as a practical matter, shut the courthouse doors on low-dollar claims where common proof plus administrable screening can protect Article III while preserving access to justice. On my pragmatic approach, the Constitution is honored by ensuring no uninjured person recovers and by denying certification when separating injured from uninjured would require individualized mini-trials—not by imposing a rigid ex ante rule that predictably harms vulnerable plaintiffs with small but real injuries.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the most serious point: a (b)(3) damages class that is materially overinclusive and lacks an administrable way to identify injury can generate improper settlement pressure and, as a practical matter, may fail predominance and superiority. But that is precisely a Rule 23 rigor problem, not a free‑standing Article III timing rule; TransUnion’s “standing to recover” holds that uninjured members cannot obtain damages, while expressly reserving when and how courts must police that in the class-action sequence. Justice Thomas’s contention that certification itself exercises judicial power over uninjured absent persons overreads what certification does—authorization to proceed does not itself award relief, and Article III is satisfied by named-plaintiff standing plus a judicially supervised, workable mechanism ensuring no uninjured person recovers. On my pragmatic textualist view, the coherent disposition is to require district courts at certification to demand a concrete, administrable winnowing plan and to deny certification when individualized injury inquiries truly predominate, rather than adopting an atextual categorical bar that the Rules and TransUnion do not supply.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that TransUnion expressly reserved the timing question and that a claims process might later screen out uninjured members—does not answer the Rule 23(b)(3) problem where individualized injury is central and no administrable, classwide method exists at certification to identify who may recover. As the Chief Justice stresses, certification is not mere “housekeeping”: it confers aggregation and settlement leverage, so postponing injury determinations that are baked into the class theory collapses predominance and superiority and risks using Rule 23 to expand the practical scope of federal adjudication in tension with the Rules Enabling Act. Justice Jackson’s administrability framing is useful, but it confirms rather than undermines the need for rigorous ex ante scrutiny when injury identification would devolve into individualized mini-trials. TransUnion’s reservation cannot be read to license certification of an overinclusive damages class on the hope that jurisdictional defects will be cured later; it leaves room only where common proof or a workable plan ensures only injured members can recover without individualized litigation swamping the case.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson make the strongest point: TransUnion expressly reserved the timing question, and in some cases a later, court-supervised winnowing process can ensure that no uninjured person recovers. But where, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the class definition and proof model at certification affirmatively sweep in substantial numbers of uninjured members without an administrable, classwide method to identify injury, the problem is not merely “when” standing is checked—it is that individualized injury becomes central and defeats Rule 23(b)(3) predominance/superiority while creating settlement pressure untethered to Article III limits. That approach enforces TransUnion’s core premise (standing to recover) without adopting Justice Thomas’s broader view that certification itself is always an unconstitutional exercise of judicial power over absent uninjured members; instead, we can take the narrow institutional course of vacating and remanding for rigorous application of TransUnion and Rule 23(b)(3) on this record. The Rules Enabling Act reinforces that we should not allow procedural aggregation to functionally enlarge who may obtain damages in federal court when the certification plan has no workable way to separate injured from uninjured.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that TransUnion reserved the timing question and that a later claims process might screen out uninjured members—matters, but it does not answer the antecedent Rule 23(b)(3) problem when the class, as certified, is structured so that injury turns on individualized inquiries with no administrable, classwide method to separate injured from uninjured. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, certification is not mere case-management; it is the judicial act that authorizes aggregate litigation and settlement leverage on behalf of absent persons, and that leverage cannot rest on a theory that would necessarily include many people who lack any right to damages in federal court. Justice Jackson’s administrability framing helps identify the right doctrinal channel—predominance, superiority, and manageability—but if the only way to ensure “standing to recover” is a multitude of individualized mini-trials, then injury is central and predominance fails rather than being a detail that can be postponed. The proper disposition remains vacatur and remand for rigorous application of TransUnion and Rule 23(b)(3) to the class definition and proof model in this case, without announcing a categorical timing rule beyond what the text and precedent require.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s settlement-pressure and Rules Enabling Act concerns are real, but they are adequately—and more textually—addressed through Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance/superiority and manageability requirements rather than by converting TransUnion’s reserved timing issue into an ex ante Article III certification bar. Justice Barrett is right that certification is not “mere housekeeping,” yet that point still does not establish that Article III requires the district court to prove injury for every absent member at certification, so long as the court rigorously demands a feasible winnowing mechanism ensuring no uninjured person recovers damages. Justice Thomas’s view that certification itself exercises unconstitutional power over uninjured absentees overstates the nature of certification, which does not adjudicate entitlement to damages and remains bounded by the court’s obligation to prevent recovery absent standing. On this pragmatic record, the administrability constraint (deny certification where identifying injury devolves into individualized mini-trials) cabins overinclusive classes without importing an atextual jurisdictional timing rule that TransUnion expressly declined to announce.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III confines the federal judicial power to resolving claims for parties who have suffered a concrete injury, and Rule 23 cannot be applied to expand that jurisdictional limit. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, each member of a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class must have Article III standing to recover damages, which strongly counsels against certifying a class that affirmatively includes uninjured members even if the Court reserved the precise timing question. Certifying such a class also threatens Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance and superiority requirements by making individualized injury determinations central and by creating undue settlement pressure untethered to injured plaintiffs’ claims. A narrow disposition would vacate and remand for application of Article III and Rule 23(b)(3) consistent with TransUnion, without adopting a rigid across-the-board rule beyond what is necessary.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III confines the federal judicial power to resolving actual “Cases” and “Controversies,” which requires a concrete injury-in-fact for each claimant seeking damages. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), every member of a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class must have Article III standing to recover, and Rule 23 cannot be applied to aggregate claims for persons who suffered no injury without exceeding constitutional limits. Because certification effectively brings absent members’ claims before the court, a class definition that affirmatively includes uninjured persons (or lacks any workable mechanism consistent with due process and the Rules Enabling Act to identify and exclude them) cannot satisfy Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance/superiority requirements. The Ninth Circuit’s approach would permit adjudication and coercive settlement pressure untethered to Article III’s original meaning, and it should be reversed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III limits the federal judicial power to resolving the claims of plaintiffs who have suffered a concrete injury, and a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class that affirmatively includes uninjured members risks exceeding that jurisdictional boundary. As TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez held, “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” and Rule 23 is only a procedural device that cannot “abridge, enlarge or modify” substantive limits on jurisdiction, see 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b). Allowing certification now while postponing standing and injury inquiries to later stages undermines Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance requirement and creates settlement pressure untethered to lawful liability. Practical consequences reinforce the constitutional point: certification should not be used to leverage aggregate damages on behalf of persons who could not sue in federal court at all.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III requires the named plaintiffs to show a concrete injury, but Rule 23(b)(3) certification should not be categorically barred merely because the class definition might sweep in some individuals who ultimately fail to prove injury; that problem can be addressed through merits adjudication and claims administration consistent with Rule 23’s predominance and superiority requirements. TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez holds that “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” but it does not compel a rigid rule that standing for each absent member must be proven at the certification stage in every case. Where the alleged discrimination plausibly caused a common, concrete harm to the class as a whole, denying certification ex ante would unduly restrict access to justice and remedial enforcement for vulnerable populations, contrary to Rule 23’s function. The proper course is to ensure that any uninjured members do not recover damages at judgment, while allowing certification when common issues predominate and mechanisms exist to separate qualifying from non-qualifying claims.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III requires that the named plaintiffs have standing and that each class member ultimately recover damages only upon proof of a concrete injury, but Rule 23(b)(3) does not categorically forbid certification merely because the class definition might encompass some persons who will fail on injury. TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez held that “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” while expressly reserving how that requirement applies at the certification stage, leaving room to treat injury as a later merits/claims-administration question where workable mechanisms can screen out uninjured claimants. The better course, consistent with Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance/superiority and statutory coherence, is to require district courts to ensure a feasible, administrable method to separate injured from uninjured (and deny certification if individualized injury issues predominate), rather than imposing an absolute jurisdictional bar to certification whenever overinclusiveness is alleged. That approach respects Article III limits without turning Rule 23 into a rigid trap that forecloses otherwise workable class proceedings where injury is common in practice and can be reliably determined.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III confines the federal judicial power to resolving cases brought by parties who have suffered a concrete injury, and this Court has said that “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages.” TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413, 431 (2021). A Rule 23(b)(3) damages class that affirmatively sweeps in uninjured persons therefore risks authorizing relief beyond the court’s jurisdiction and, as Cordoba and its progeny recognize, raises a predominance problem because individualized proof of injury (standing) will tend to overwhelm common issues. Rule 23 is a procedural rule and cannot enlarge Article III limits, so certification cannot proceed on the premise that uninjured members can be sorted out only after classwide liability is determined. Consistent with separation-of-powers principles and the Rules Enabling Act’s constraint that procedure not alter substantive rights, the certification order should be set aside to the extent it includes uninjured class members in a (b)(3) damages class.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III confines the federal judicial power to resolving concrete disputes brought by plaintiffs who have suffered an injury in fact, and Rule 23 cannot be applied in a manner that authorizes adjudication or damages awards for persons lacking standing. TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez held that “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” and although it reserved the precise timing question at certification, a Rule 23(b)(3) class definition that affirmatively sweeps in substantial numbers of uninjured members raises serious constitutional and Rule 23(b)(3) predominance/superiority problems because individualized injury inquiries would overwhelm common issues and undermine workability. Consistent with Amchem’s insistence on rigorous adherence to Rule 23’s limits and the Rules Enabling Act’s constraint that procedural rules not alter substantive rights, certification should be reversed where the class mechanism cannot reliably separate injured from uninjured members without devolving into individualized proceedings. Judicial restraint and institutional legitimacy counsel applying TransUnion’s standing principle and traditional limits on federal jurisdiction rather than permitting overbroad aggregate damages classes that risk binding parties and coercing settlement beyond Article III’s bounds.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III limits the federal judicial power to resolving concrete cases and controversies, and that constraint applies in class actions no less than in individual suits. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” and Rule 23 cannot be used to aggregate claims for persons who suffered no injury-in-fact without exceeding constitutional limits. A Rule 23(b)(3) damages class that affirmatively includes uninjured members also implicates predominance and superiority because identifying who was injured becomes an individualized merits inquiry that cannot be deferred without risking that the class device enlarges substantive rights, contrary to the Rules Enabling Act. Given TransUnion’s instruction that federal courts lack power to award relief to uninjured plaintiffs, certification of a damages class that necessarily sweeps in such persons is improper.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III requires that named plaintiffs have standing and that any class member who ultimately recovers damages show a concrete injury, but TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez expressly left open whether every class member must demonstrate standing at the class-certification stage. In a Rule 23(b)(3) case, the proper inquiry is whether common issues (including injury and liability) predominate and whether class treatment is superior, Fed. R. Civ. P. 23(b)(3); if a small number of putatively uninjured persons may be screened out through merits proof or a claims-administration process, that typically goes to manageability rather than a categorical jurisdictional bar. Given the respondents’ framing that the challenged practice inflicted a common discriminatory injury on the class, I would not treat the mere possibility of some uninjured members as dispositive at certification absent a showing that individualized injury inquiries overwhelm common proof. This approach respects Article III’s limits while promoting procedural fairness and practical administration of civil-rights claims without creating an overbroad, formalistic standing rule untethered from Rule 23’s text.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court may certify a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class when the class definition includes individuals who suffered no Article III injury.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. III (standing/injury-in-fact requirement) as applied to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(b)(3) class certification (and, in the underlying discrimination suit, federal disability-discrimination law such as the ADA, though the question presented centers on Article III + Rule 23).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Labcorp argues that Article III limits federal courts to resolving actual cases or controversies for injured plaintiffs, and that those limits apply to every member of a certified damages class—not merely the named representatives. Because Rule 23(b)(3) authorizes aggregation for efficiency but does not expand constitutional jurisdiction, a class that includes uninjured members is impermissible (or at least cannot be certified as defined). Labcorp contends that allowing uninjured individuals into the class (i) transforms the action into an advisory, non-justiciable proceeding as to those persons, (ii) improperly inflates leverage and settlement pressure, and (iii) creates unmanageable merits and damages issues because injury would have to be litigated through individualized proceedings after certification. It further maintains that Supreme Court review properly targets the Ninth Circuit’s judgment affirming certification (not any particular phrasing of a class definition used at intermediate points), invoking the principle that the Court reviews judgments, not statements in opinions (as reflected in the cited Amgen v. Sanofi language).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the Ninth Circuit correctly affirmed certification because the certified classes consist of people injured by disability discrimination (i.e., the classes are not meaningfully ‘uninjured’), and that Article III is satisfied so long as the named plaintiffs have standing and the class is properly certified under Rule 23. In their view, disputes about whether some class members ultimately prove injury are merits and proof questions that can be handled through class-member identification, claims processes, or individualized damages/injury determinations after liability is decided, without turning certification itself into a member-by-member standing inquiry. They also resist Labcorp’s effort to reframe the case as involving a materially different class definition than the one actually affirmed, characterizing Labcorp’s arguments as either forfeited or outside the Court’s jurisdictional focus depending on which definition is considered.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress TransUnion’s footnote reserving the timing question and to warn against turning certification into a member-by-member standing trial. But as Justice Kagan explains, that reservation does not license a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class whose definition and proof plan predictably sweep in substantial numbers of uninjured persons without an administrable, objective method to separate them; that is a predominance/manageability failure that also implicates Article III and the Rules Enabling Act. A narrow disposition—vacate and remand for a refined class definition and workable common proof or screening mechanism—respects TransUnion’s core holding (no damages to uninjured members) without announcing a rigid “standing must be proved for each absentee at certification” rule. Justice Gorsuch’s constitutional framing reinforces the limits on judicial power, but institutional legitimacy counsels resolving this case on the narrower Rule 23/workability ground while making clear that any recovery must be limited to injured members.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that TransUnion reserved the timing question in footnote 4 and that absent members’ injuries might be sorted out later through administration, but Article III’s text confines the “judicial Power” to actual cases and controversies and does not permit certifying a damages class framed to include persons who suffered no concrete injury. TransUnion’s holding that “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages” means a federal court cannot, consistent with its limited jurisdiction, approve a mechanism that predictably adjudicates and pressures settlement based on claims that are not justiciable for many members. As Justice Gorsuch and the Chief Justice emphasize, Rule 23 and the Rules Enabling Act cannot be used to enlarge jurisdiction or abridge a defendant’s substantive right not to pay damages to uninjured claimants; if injury cannot be shown by workable common proof at certification, that is a predominance/manageability failure as well as an Article III problem. I would reverse (or at least vacate and remand) to require a class definition and certification findings that reliably exclude uninjured individuals rather than treating standing as a post-certification claims-processing issue.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press TransUnion’s footnote 4 reserving the timing question, but that reservation cannot be read to permit certification of a concededly overbroad damages class and then treating Article III as a post-certification claims-processing issue. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, whatever the precise moment for resolving each absent member’s standing, Rule 23(b)(3) still requires at certification a workable, objective method and class definition that does not predictably sweep in more than a de minimis number of uninjured persons; otherwise predominance, manageability, and settlement leverage become untethered to concrete injury. Justice Gorsuch’s point reinforces the constitutional boundary: Rule 23 and the Rules Enabling Act cannot be used to enlarge federal jurisdiction or effectively compel payments to persons with no justiciable claim. I therefore remain with petitioner and favor vacatur and remand for a narrowed class definition and proof plan rather than an inflexible member-by-member standing trial at certification.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively warn that a (b)(3) damages class should not be certified on a definition and proof plan that predictably sweeps in substantial numbers of uninjured people, because that distorts settlement leverage and signals predominance/manageability defects. But TransUnion’s footnote 4 matters: it expressly reserved when absent class members’ standing must be shown, and I do not read Article III as requiring the certification stage to function as a member-by-member jurisdictional adjudication rather than a Rule 23 fit inquiry. The constitutional core is that the named plaintiffs present a concrete dispute and that the court ultimately awards damages only to those with standing; requiring objective screening mechanisms and excluding uninjured claimants from recovery can satisfy TransUnion without broadly foreclosing certification whenever injury identification requires later administration. The Rules Enabling Act concern, as framed by Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett, is real, but it is met by remedial safeguards (no payment to uninjured members) and Rule 23 rigor, not by converting standing into a categorical bar at certification that would undercut access to justice in systemic harm cases.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press TransUnion’s footnote reserving the timing of absent-member standing, and I agree Article III does not require a member-by-member standing trial at certification. But as Chief Justice Roberts frames it, Rule 23(b)(3) still demands a workable, predominantly common method and an administrable class definition; if the certified class predictably sweeps in substantial uninjured persons with no objective screening mechanism, that is a predominance/manageability failure that also risks authorizing settlement pressure and damages exposure untethered to concrete injury. That approach respects TransUnion’s core holding—no damages for uninjured class members—without announcing an inflexible “zero uninjured members” rule or converting standing into a post-certification claims-processing afterthought. On my pragmatic textualist view, vacatur and remand for a refined class definition and proof plan is the narrow, coherent path.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize TransUnion’s footnote 4 reserving the timing question, and I agree Article III does not compel a member-by-member standing trial at the Rule 23 stage. But that reservation cannot be read to allow certification of a damages class defined in a way that predictably includes substantial numbers of uninjured persons without any workable, objective method to screen them out—because Rule 23 cannot enlarge the judicial power beyond a real “case or controversy,” and the Rules Enabling Act bars procedural aggregation from altering the substantive requirement of concrete injury for damages. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, when injury cannot be shown by predominantly common, administrable proof, the defect is not mere “claims administration”; it signals predominance/manageability failure and risks advisory adjudication plus settlement leverage untethered to justiciable claims. The appropriate course remains vacatur and remand for a narrowed class definition and proof plan that reliably confines the damages class to injured members, consistent with TransUnion’s core holding.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press TransUnion’s footnote reserving the timing question and the practical value of later claims administration, especially in civil-rights enforcement. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, even if Article III does not require member-by-member standing mini-trials at certification, a (b)(3) damages class still must be defined and supported by a workable, objective method that does not predictably sweep in substantial numbers of uninjured persons; otherwise the certification order authorizes a damages proceeding (and settlement leverage) untethered to concrete injury, in tension with TransUnion’s core holding and the Rules Enabling Act. I therefore favor the narrow institutional path Roberts outlines: vacate and remand for a refined class definition and proof plan that reliably cabins the class to injured members, rather than adopting an inflexible “zero uninjured members” rule. Sotomayor’s approach treats Article III as curable through post-certification processing, but on my view the constitutional and predominance problems arise precisely when injury is not administrably provable on a classwide basis at the outset.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to emphasize TransUnion’s footnote reserving the timing question and to resist turning certification into member-by-member standing trials, but that reservation cannot be read to permit certification of a damages class that—by its definition and proof plan—predictably includes substantial numbers of uninjured people with no administrable way to screen them out. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, that defect is simultaneously constitutional and Rule 23(b)(3) workability/predominance: injury becomes an individualized gatekeeping issue, and the certification order effectively authorizes a damages adjudication (and settlement pressure) beyond Article III’s case-or-controversy limit. The Rules Enabling Act reinforces the point: Rule 23 cannot be used to alter the substantive requirement of concrete injury for each damages claimant or to enlarge the court’s jurisdiction by aggregating nonjusticiable claims. A narrow vacatur-and-remand requiring a refined class definition and a workable, objective method to identify injured members best respects TransUnion’s reservation while keeping the proceedings within constitutional bounds.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press TransUnion’s footnote reservation and the real-world value of allowing Rule 23 mechanisms to vindicate systemic harms without turning certification into a member-by-member standing trial. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, even if Article III does not require individualized standing determinations at certification, Rule 23(b)(3) still demands a workable, predominantly common method for identifying who was actually injured; otherwise injury becomes the central individualized issue and predominance/superiority collapse. From a procedural-fairness, consequence-focused perspective, certifying a damages class that predictably sweeps in a substantial number of uninjured people—without an administrable screening method—unfairly magnifies settlement pressure and risks payouts untethered to concrete harm, which TransUnion forbids. A narrow vacatur and remand for a tightened class definition or reliable proof plan preserves access to justice while keeping the class device aligned with both Article III limits and practical manageability.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III confines the federal courts to resolving concrete disputes, and Rule 23 cannot enlarge that constitutional jurisdiction in a damages class action. As TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez held, "[e]very class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages," and the inclusion of uninjured persons in a Rule 23(b)(3) class definition threatens to convert the proceeding into an impermissible adjudication as to those individuals while also distorting Rule 23(b)(3) predominance through individualized injury inquiries. Although TransUnion reserved the precise timing question at certification, a minimally sufficient showing at the certification stage is required that the class is defined and can be proven in a way that does not sweep in more than a de minimis number of uninjured members, consistent with Article III and the Rules Enabling Act’s limit that procedural rules not abridge substantive rights. A narrow disposition would therefore vacate the certification and remand for a class definition and method of proof that reliably confines the damages class to members who suffered an Article III injury.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article III confines the federal judicial power to real "Cases" and "Controversies," and a plaintiff must show an injury in fact; Rule 23 is a procedural device that cannot enlarge that constitutional jurisdiction. In a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class, "[e]very class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages," TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413, 431 (2021), and certifying a class defined to include uninjured persons risks adjudicating claims for those who lack a concrete injury. Because the Rules Enabling Act and Rule 23 cannot abridge a defendant’s substantive rights or transform an Article III court into a forum for advisory opinions, the class must be defined (and shown through a workable method at certification) to exclude uninjured individuals. Accordingly, I would reverse the certification to the extent it includes members who suffered no Article III injury.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Article III confines the federal judicial power to resolving concrete disputes for plaintiffs who have suffered an injury in fact, and Rule 23 cannot expand that constitutional jurisdiction. As TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez holds, “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” and a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class that includes uninjured members necessarily asks the federal courts to adjudicate (and leverage settlement pressure from) claims outside the case-or-controversy requirement. Practically, certifying such a class also undermines Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance and superiority requirements by guaranteeing individualized injury inquiries later and inflating coercive classwide exposure unrelated to actual injury. The Ninth Circuit’s approach, by permitting certification notwithstanding the inclusion of uninjured individuals, risks converting federal courts into venues for advisory proceedings as to those persons, contrary to Article III.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Article III requires an injury-in-fact for those who seek damages, but it does not demand a member-by-member standing adjudication as a prerequisite to Rule 23(b)(3) certification so long as the named plaintiffs have standing and Rule 23’s predominance and manageability requirements are satisfied. TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez held that “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” 594 U.S. 413, 423 (2021), but it expressly reserved how to handle absent class members’ standing at the certification stage, id. at 431 n.4, leaving room for courts to address injury through common proof, claims administration, or later proceedings without collapsing certification into individualized mini-trials. Where (as respondents contend) the class is defined around persons subjected to the discriminatory practice, excluding the truly uninjured is a remedial and administrative task consistent with Rule 23 rather than a jurisdictional bar to certification. A rigid rule forbidding certification whenever a class definition could include some uninjured persons would unduly impair enforcement of civil-rights protections (including disability-discrimination law) and access to justice for vulnerable plaintiffs, contrary to Rule 23’s purpose and the practical realities of proving systemic discrimination.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Article III limits federal courts to resolving concrete disputes for parties who have suffered an injury-in-fact, and Rule 23 cannot enlarge that constitutional jurisdiction. TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez makes clear that “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” and a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class defined to include uninjured persons risks authorizing adjudication and monetary relief for claimants who are not part of any “case or controversy.” Even if TransUnion reserved in a footnote the precise timing question at certification, Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance/superiority requirements and basic workability point the same way: if the class definition sweeps in substantial numbers of uninjured individuals without an administrable method to separate them, certification is improper. The Ninth Circuit’s approach threatens to convert standing into a post-certification claims-processing problem and to magnify settlement pressure disconnected from the merits, contrary to Article III and the limits implicit in Rule 23.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article III confines the federal “judicial Power” to resolving concrete disputes for parties who have suffered an injury in fact, and Rule 23 cannot enlarge that constitutional boundary. As TransUnion explains, “Article III does not give federal courts the power to order relief to any uninjured plaintiff, class action or not,” and it follows that a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class may not be certified (at least as defined) when it includes members who suffered no concrete injury because the court would be authorizing adjudication and potential relief beyond its jurisdiction. This conclusion also accords with the Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b), which bars procedural rules from abridging, enlarging, or modifying substantive rights, and with the separation-of-powers imperative that courts not issue advisory judgments. If identifying injury for many class members requires individualized proceedings, that is not a reason to overlook Article III but a signal that predominance and manageability are lacking for certification as framed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Article III confines federal courts to resolving concrete disputes for injured plaintiffs, and Rule 23(b)(3) cannot expand that constitutional limit. Under TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” and a class definition that affirmatively sweeps in uninjured persons risks authorizing relief to those who lack injury-in-fact, contrary to Article III and the principle that class actions “add nothing to the question of standing.” Practical workability also cuts against certification where no administrable method exists to separate injured from uninjured members without devolving into individualized mini-trials, undermining Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance/superiority framework. Consistent with judicial restraint and precedent, the proper course is to require class definitions (or certification findings) that ensure only injured persons are included for damages purposes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III’s text confines the federal judicial power to “Cases” and “Controversies,” which requires a concrete injury-in-fact; Rule 23 is a procedural device and cannot enlarge that constitutional limit. As TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez held, “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” and a Rule 23(b)(3) damages class definition that affirmatively sweeps in uninjured persons therefore risks authorizing relief for those outside Article III’s ambit. Even if TransUnion reserved the precise timing question at certification, Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance and manageability inquiries cannot be satisfied where injury is not susceptible to classwide proof and must be sorted through individualized proceedings for a substantial share of the class. Precedent respecting the Rules Enabling Act’s limit on procedural rules reinforces that Rule 23 may not be used to aggregate claims in a way that effectively dispenses with the injury requirement for absent class members.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Article III’s case-or-controversy limitation requires a concrete injury-in-fact for each claimant seeking damages, and Rule 23(b)(3) cannot expand federal jurisdiction to encompass claims by uninjured persons. TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez held that “every class member must have Article III standing in order to recover individual damages,” and although it reserved how courts should address that issue at certification, a (b)(3) damages class defined to include uninjured members creates serious procedural-fairness and practical-administration problems under predominance/superiority because individualized injury inquiries would overwhelm the class device. A court may not certify a class in a form that predictably necessitates post-certification adjudication for many uninjured claimants, both because that risks advisory adjudication as to those persons and because it improperly leverages settlement pressure without a workable, fair mechanism to separate injured from uninjured members. The proper course is to require a class definition (or a certification record) that ensures membership is limited by objective criteria tightly linked to injury, consistent with Article III and Rule 23(b)(3)’s manageability and predominance requirements.
